'''''Abies amabilis''''', commonly known as the '''Pacific silver fir''', is a [[fir]] native to the [[Pacific Northwest]] of [[North America]], occurring in the [[Pacific Coast Ranges]] and the [[Cascade Range]]. It is also commonly referred to in English as the '''white fir''', '''red fir''', '''lovely fir''', '''amabilis fir''', '''Cascades fir''', or '''silver fir'''.<ref name=gd/><ref name=pm/>

==Description==
The tree is a large evergreen [[conifer]] growing to {{convert|30–50|m|abbr=off}}, exceptionally {{convert|72|m|abbr=on}} tall,<ref name=gd/><ref name="tktimb">{{Cite book |last1=Turner |first1=Mark |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VLbAAwAAQBAJ |title=Trees & Shrubs of the Pacific Northwest |last2=Kuhlmann |first2=Ellen |date=2014 |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |isbn=978-1-60469-263-1 |edition=1st |location=Portland, OR |page=58}}</ref> and with a trunk diameter of up to {{convert|1.2|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}}, exceptionally {{convert|2.3|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}}. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] on younger trees is light grey, thin and covered with [[resin]] blisters.<ref name="Arno-2020">{{Cite book |last1=Arno |first1=Stephen F. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qDD4DwAAQBAJ |title=Northwest Trees: Identifying & Understanding the Region's Native Trees |last2=Hammerly |first2=Ramona P. |publisher=[[Mountaineers Books]] |year=2020 |isbn=978-1-68051-329-5 |edition=field guide |location=Seattle |pages=123–128 |language=en |oclc=1141235469 |orig-date=1977}}</ref> On older trees, it darkens and develops scales and furrows. The [[leaves]] are needle-like, flattened, {{convert|1|-|4.5|cm|frac=8}} long and {{convert|2|mm|frac=16}} wide by {{convert|0.5|mm|abbr=on|frac=32|2}} thick, dark green above,<ref name=tktimb /> and with two white bands of [[stoma]]ta below, and slightly notched at the tip.<ref name=fna/> The leaf arrangement is spiral on the shoot, but with each leaf variably twisted at the base so they lie flat to either side of and above the shoot, with none below the shoot. The shoots are orange-red with dense velvety pubescence.<ref name="Arno-2020" />

The [[conifer cone|cones]] are {{convert|8–17|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long and {{convert|4|–|6|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} broad, dark purple before maturity;<ref name=tktimb /><ref name="Arno-2020" /> the scale bracts are short, and hidden in the closed cone. The brownish winged [[seed]]s are {{Convert|3.5|mm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long<ref name=tktimb /> and released when the cones disintegrate at maturity about 6–7 months after pollination.

The tree can live to over 400 years old.<ref name="Arno-2020" /> The oldest known individual, on [[Mount Cain]], was about 920 years old when it was sampled.<ref>{{cite web |date=1997–2025 |first=Christopher J. |last=Earle |title=Abies amabilis |website=The Gymnosperm Database |url=https://www.conifers.org/pi/Abies_amabilis.php}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first1=Roberta |last1=Parish |first2=Joseph A. |last2=Antos |title=Structure and dynamics of an ancient montane forest in coastal British Columbia |doi=10.1007/s00442-004-1690-4 |journal=Oecologia |date=2004 |issn=0029-8549 |volume=141 |issue=4 |pages=562–576 |pmid=15322898 }}</ref>{{rp|568}}

=== Similar species ===
Pacific silver fir is very closely related to [[Abies mariesii|''A. mariesii'']] (Maries' fir) from [[Japan]], which is distinguished by its slightly shorter leaves, being {{convert|1.5|-|2.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long, and smaller cones, which are {{convert|5|–|11|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long.<ref name="Rushforth">{{cite book |last1=Rushforth |first1=Keith D. |last2=Rushforth |first2=K. |title=Conifers |publisher=Helm |publication-place=London |date=1987 |isbn=0-7470-2801-X |pages=77–78}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Xiang |first1=Qiao-Ping |last2=Wei |first2=Ran |last3=Shao |first3=Yi-Zhen |last4=Yang |first4=Zu-Yu |last5=Wang |first5=Xiao-Quan |last6=Zhang |first6=Xian-Chun |title=Phylogenetic relationships, possible ancient hybridization, and biogeographic history of ''Abies'' (Pinaceae) based on data from nuclear, plastid, and mitochondrial genomes |journal=Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution |volume=82 |date=2015 |doi=10.1016/j.ympev.2014.10.008 |pages=1–14 |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1055790314003595 |access-date=2026-05-16|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Etymology==
The species name is [[Latin]] for 'lovely'.<ref name=gd/>

== Distribution and ecology ==
[[File:Abies amabilis 26395.JPG|thumb|Cone growing in the [[Pacific Northwest]]]]

The species is native to the [[Pacific Northwest]] of North America, occurring in the [[Pacific Coast Ranges]] and the [[Cascade Range]] from the extreme southeast of [[Alaska]], through western [[British Columbia]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]] and [[Oregon]], to the extreme northwest of [[California]]. It grows from sea level to {{convert|1000|m|abbr=on}} in the north of the range, and to {{convert|610|–|2000|m|abbr=on}} in the south of the range. Populations on the east slope of the Cascades are confined to elevations above {{convert|1000|m|abbr=on}} in Washington and {{convert|1160|m|abbr=on}} in Oregon.<ref name="Silvics">{{Silvics |volume = 1 |genus = Abies |species = amabilis |first1 = Peggy D. |last1 = Crawford |first2 = Chadwick Dearing |last2 = Oliver |access-date = 23 April 2023}}</ref>

It is always found in [[temperate rainforest]]s with relatively high precipitation and cool, humid summers. Growing in dense stands, it prospers in [[Shade tolerance|shade]] and snow.<ref name="Arno-2020" /> Common associate trees are [[Tsuga heterophylla|western hemlock]] in northern ranges, [[Douglas-fir]]<ref name="Arno-2020" /> in central areas, and [[California buckeye]] in the extreme southern area of its range.<ref name="hogan2008" /> Western hemlock is equally shade tolerant, but Pacific silver fir saplings are more resilient of ground obstacles.<ref name="Arno-2020" /> Though its thin bark makes it susceptible to fire, the slow-growing saplings succeed less shade-tolerant species.<ref name="Arno-2020" /> It survives well at high elevation, but eventually succumbs to [[Root rot|root]] or [[heart rot]], in addition to diseases and insects such as ''[[Adelges piceae]]''.<ref name="Arno-2020" />

On northeastern Vancouver Island, Pacific silver fir grows along with western hemlock in dense forests with sparse understory vegetation. Another type of forest dominated by [[western redcedar]] and western hemlock with more open canopies and an understories composed primarily of salal (''[[Gaultheria shallon]]'') also occurs in the area. The two forest types occur in areas with very similar environmental conditions and are separated by sharp boundaries, often less than {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}} wide. Western redcedar [[recruitment (biology)|recruitment]] is nearly absent in the western hemlock–Pacific silver fir forest type, and there is no evidence of a transitional stage between the two types. It has been hypothesized that, once established, these forest types are self-sustaining and are unlikely to change unless a major [[disturbance (ecology)|disturbance]] occurs.<ref>{{cite journal |last1 = Weber |first1 = Adrian |last2 = Kimmins |first2 = J. P. |last3 = Gilbert |first3 = Benjamin |last4 = Lo |first4 = Yueh-Hsin |last5 = Blanco |first5 = Juan A. |date = October 2014 |title = Multiple-pathway succession in coastal ''Tsuga heterophylla'', ''Thuja plicata'', and ''Abies amabilis'' forests on northeastern Vancouver Island, British Columbia |journal = [[Canadian Journal of Forest Research]] |publisher = [[Canadian Science Publishing]] |volume = 44 |issue = 10 |pages = 1145{{ndash}}1155 |doi = 10.1139/cjfr-2014-0060|bibcode = 2014CaJFR..44.1145W |hdl = 2454/19816 |hdl-access = free }}</ref>

== Uses ==
Indigenous Nations, including the [[Nuxalk]], [[Haisla people|Haisla]], and [[Kitasoo]], used ''A. amabilis'' for medicinal purposes.<ref name="Arno-2020" /> Ethnobotanist Daniel Moerman notes, for example, that Nuxalk Peoples mixed mountain goat tallow with liquid pitch to treat sore throat. An infusion of bark, by contrast, may have been used to address stomach issues.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Moerman |first=Daniel |title=Native American Ethnobotany |publisher=Timber Press, Inc. |year=2020 |isbn=978-0-88192-453-4 |edition=14th |location=Portland, Oregon |pages=33}}</ref>

In addition to medicinal uses, hardened pitch of the plant was sometimes chewed for pleasure by the [[Ditidaht First Nation|Ditidaht Peoples]].<ref name=":0" /> The foliage has an attractive scent and was admired for its scent long before the arrival of European settlers in its native range. The Ditidaht brought boughs into their homes as an air freshener, whereas [[Nlakaʼpamux]] peoples boiled boughs to create unique plant-based hair perfumes.<ref name=":0" />

The [[wood]] is soft and not very strong; settlers thus tended to use this species for [[paper]] making, packing crates, and other cheap construction work.<ref name="Arno-2020" /> The lumber is often paired with that of western hemlock.<ref name="Arno-2020" />

Seeds were not brought to Europe for cultivation until the 19th century, when [[David Douglas (botanist)|David Douglas]] first transported seed to Britain in 1830.<ref name="Arno-2020" /><ref name=Mitchell>{{cite book |last=Mitchell |first=Alan F. |title=The Trees of Britain and Northern Europe Collins |publisher=Collins |publication-place=London |date=1982 |isbn=0-00-219037-0 |pages=57, 266}}</ref> Today, the tree is sometimes planted as an [[ornamental tree]] in parks and large gardens, though its requirement for cool, humid summers limits its optimal areas; successful growth away from its native range is restricted to areas like western [[Scotland]] and southern [[New Zealand]].<ref name="Rushforth"/><ref name=Mitchell/> Pacific silver fir is sometimes used for [[Christmas]] decoration, including [[Christmas tree]]s.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}
